claims.text: A coupled machine-learning and first-principles simulation can separately predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr.
The coupled approach will reduce prediction error by 20–30% relative to Debye- or DFT-elastic-constant-based approaches.
Machine-learned force fields can capture realistic phonon-lifetime distributions.
Concurrent DFT calculations can determine temperature-dependent electron-scattering rates for HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are expected to be nearly equal.
Intrinsic chemical disorder in HfNbTaTiZr is associated with local lattice distortions.
Chemical disorder and lattice distortions modify local interatomic force constants.
Chemical disorder and lattice distortions modify electron-scattering pathways.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen further influences the lattice distortions, force constants, or electron-scattering pathways.
On-the-fly training of interatomic potentials accurately resolves phonon propagation and lifetimes.
Combining learned phonon dynamics with first-principles electron scattering enables transport-channel decoupling without a single Debye temperature.
In oxygen-doped HfNbTaTiZr at 300–1200 K, total thermal conductivity will be 10–17 W/(m K).
Existing comparison methods use modified Debye-temperature estimates or DFT-derived elastic properties.
The existing comparison calculations represent idealized, defect-free bulk crystals.
The proposed model is restricted to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with controlled defects, up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, and the specified temperature windows.
Performance outside the specified composition and temperature windows is untested.
Wiedemann–Franz analysis and phonon spectroscopy can provide experimentally separated electronic and lattice conductivities for validation.
The hypothesis is falsified if either predicted channel differs from experiment by more than 30%, or if low-temperature parity is absent.
